reprokit

Sometimes the raw data behind a paper cannot be shared, for example because participants did not consent to it. Readers then have no way to reproduce the results, and no way to tell whether the reported numbers fit together. reprokit helps from both sides, using the same summary statistics. If you are the author, it tells you whether summary statistics are enough for readers to reproduce your result exactly, stores them, and writes an appendix that lists them and what readers lose by not having the raw data. If you are the reader, it tests whether the reported numbers are consistent with each other, taking rounding into account.

Sharing raw data remains the standard. appendix() records the reason you give for not sharing the raw data; without one, it says the author did not state one, and reprokit never suggests a reason. reprokit does not make withholding data easier to justify; it makes the minimum you owe your readers explicit.

reprokit needs R >= 4.1 and depends only on base R (stats, utils).

Documentation: https://dm-k1.github.io/reprokit/

Installation

reprokit is not on CRAN. Install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("dm-k1/reprokit")

# or
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("dm-k1/reprokit")

The vignettes are not built by default. To get them, install with:

pak::pak("dm-k1/reprokit", dependencies = TRUE, build_vignettes = TRUE)
# or
remotes::install_github("dm-k1/reprokit", build_vignettes = TRUE)

Then open them with vignette("reprokit"). Without installing, read them on the website or as sources on GitHub: reprokit.Rmd, concepts.Rmd, validation.Rmd.

Author path: you cannot share the raw data

sufficient_stats() says whether summaries suffice. It never errors on the verdict, which is one of:

  • apa_suffices: the numbers APA style asks for determine the reported results exactly.
  • apa_plus_suffices: a few numbers beyond APA style are needed (for the paired t-test, the correlation between conditions). The advice names each one, says why, and gives the range the APA numbers imply.
  • needs_raw_data: summaries do not suffice, or the groups are so small that summaries are almost the data.

Every verdict says that sharing the raw data remains the standard (APA Publication Manual section 1.14, Ethics Code 8.14). You can also get a verdict from typed numbers alone, without a model or data: sufficient_stats(test = "paired", n = "30", m = c("5.1", "4.6"), sd = c("1.2", "1.3")).

The printed object narrates the verdict, what to publish, what readers lose, and which group or cell a disclosure flag fired for. It stores the statistics at full precision:

library(reprokit)

s <- sufficient_stats(extra ~ group, data = sleep, test = "welch")
s
#> <reprokit sufficient_stats>  analysis: independent-samples t-test  (input: formula)
#> Verdict: apa_suffices
#> Because: Summary statistics suffice: per-group n, mean and SD determine the reported results exactly.
#> The numbers APA style asks a paper to report suffice to reproduce this analysis exactly.
#> To publish: per-group n, mean and SD (appendix() writes this out).
#> Disclosure check: passed (group sizes, threshold 5).
#> What readers lose compared with the raw data:
#>   * checking the distribution and outliers within each group
#>   * nonparametric or robust alternatives
#> Statistics stored: n, mean, sd
#> Sharing the raw data remains the standard (APA Publication Manual section 1.14, Ethics Code 8.14).

appendix() writes the appendix for your paper (Markdown, ready to paste). Underneath, it reproduces the result from the stored statistics and refuses if it does not match your analysis. sharing_reason is optional:

appendix(s, choices = list(convention = "pooled"),
         sharing_reason = "Consent did not cover public sharing.")
#> ## Appendix: sufficient statistics for the independent-samples t-test
#> 
#> The APA Publication Manual (7th ed.) asks for "sufficient information to help readers fully understand the analyses conducted" (§3.7) and for data that "allow readers to confirm the basic reported analyses" (§6.43). When that set is extensive, "the information could be supplied in a supplementary data set or an appendix" (§3.7). This is that appendix.
#> 
#> ### A. The numbers APA style asks for
#> 
#> |  | group 1 | group 2 |
#> | --- | --- | --- |
#> | n | 10 | 10 |
#> | M | 0.75 | 2.33 |
#> | SD | 1.79 | 2.00 |
#> 
#> | Result | Value |
#> | --- | --- |
#> | t(17.78) | −1.86 |
#> | p | .079 |
#> | d, Cohen's d (pooled SD) | −0.83 |
#> | 95% CI of the mean difference (group 1 − group 2) | [−3.37, 0.21] |
#> 
#> ### B. Numbers APA does not require that the result needs
#> 
#> None: the APA numbers in block A determine the result.
#> 
#> ### C. Analysis choices
#> 
#> | Choice | Answer |
#> | --- | --- |
#> | Tails | two-sided |
#> | Confidence level | 95% |
#> | Test | Welch's t |
#> | Effect-size convention | Cohen's d (pooled SD) (declaring it is a reprokit rule; APA does not require it) |
#> 
#> ### D. APA numbers a reader cannot check from these statistics
#> 
#> None: every number in block A follows from blocks A and B.
#> 
#> ### Raw data
#> 
#> Reason for not sharing the raw data: Consent did not cover public sharing.
#> 
#> **What readers lose compared with the raw data:**
#> 
#> - checking the distribution and outliers within each group
#> - nonparametric or robust alternatives
#> 
#> **Disclosure check.** No summary rests on fewer than 5 cases, and n is at least 10. Checked: group sizes. This lowers the risk of identifying a participant; it does not remove it.

Further numbers the appendix does not print by default (eta squared, omega squared, R squared, standardized betas, and so on) are added with extra: names, or "all".

x <- strsplit(paste(appendix(s, choices = list(convention = "pooled"), extra = c("r2", "omega2"),
                  sharing_reason = "Consent did not cover public sharing."), collapse = "\n"), "\n")[[1]]
cat(x[seq(grep("Additional numbers", x), grep("Raw data", x) - 1)], sep = "\n")
#> ### Additional numbers
#> 
#> Computed from the stored summaries at the author's request.
#> 
#> | Number | Value |
#> | --- | --- |
#> | R² | .16 |
#> | ω² | .11 |

From your fitted result

You can pass the result you already have. A t.test() or cor.test() result needs its data; an lm, aov or chisq.test() result does not. The choices the result records (tails, confidence level, Student or Welch, continuity correction) are read from it and marked as such.

sufficient_stats(t.test(extra ~ group, data = sleep), data = sleep)
#> <reprokit sufficient_stats>  analysis: independent-samples t-test  (input: t.test)
#> Verdict: apa_suffices
#> Because: Summary statistics suffice: per-group n, mean and SD determine the reported results exactly.
#> The numbers APA style asks a paper to report suffice to reproduce this analysis exactly.
#> To publish: per-group n, mean and SD (appendix() writes this out).
#> Disclosure check: passed (group sizes, threshold 5).
#> Choices read from the t.test result: test = Welch.
#> What readers lose compared with the raw data:
#>   * checking the distribution and outliers within each group
#>   * nonparametric or robust alternatives
#> Statistics stored: n, mean, sd
#> Sharing the raw data remains the standard (APA Publication Manual section 1.14, Ethics Code 8.14).
sufficient_stats(aov(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth))
#> <reprokit sufficient_stats>  analysis: one-way ANOVA  (input: aov)
#> Verdict: apa_suffices
#> Because: Summary statistics suffice: per-group n, mean and SD determine the reported results exactly.
#> The numbers APA style asks a paper to report suffice to reproduce this analysis exactly.
#> To publish: per-group n, mean and SD (appendix() writes this out).
#> Disclosure check: passed (group sizes, threshold 5).
#> What readers lose compared with the raw data:
#>   * checking the distribution and outliers within each group
#>   * checking equal variances beyond the group SDs
#>   * post-hoc comparisons that need the raw data or the error term of a model
#> Statistics stored: n, mean, sd
#> Sharing the raw data remains the standard (APA Publication Manual section 1.14, Ethics Code 8.14).
sufficient_stats(chisq.test(table(mtcars$am, mtcars$vs)))$verdict
#> [1] "apa_suffices"

For a mediation, give the two regressions: sufficient_stats(lm(M ~ X, data = d), lm(Y ~ X + M, data = d)).

The appendix lists the numbers APA style asks for, any further numbers a reader needs, the analysis choices you made (tails, confidence level, which test, which effect-size convention), the numbers a reader cannot check from these statistics, why the raw data are not shared, what readers lose, and a disclosure check on small groups.

Reader path: you are reading a paper

Pass the reported numbers as strings, so the decimals count: "2.85" means anything from 2.845 to 2.855.

check_reported("welch",
               n = c("10", "10"), m = c("0.75", "2.33"), sd = c("1.79", "2.00"),
               t = "-1.86", df = "17.8", p = ".079")
#> The analysis is consistent with the reported statistics.
#> Level 3: the sufficient set is reported (the numbers contain everything needed to reproduce the analysis; that is not itself a check).
#> Variants that fit: two-sided
#> Tests that fit: Welch's t
#> 
#>  quantity   reported   status                checked_against
#>         n     10, 10 coherent df_from_n; t_from_descriptives
#>         m 0.75, 2.33 coherent            t_from_descriptives
#>        sd 1.79, 2.00 coherent df_from_n; t_from_descriptives
#>         t      -1.86 verified  t_from_descriptives; p_from_t
#>        df       17.8 verified            df_from_n; p_from_t
#>         p       .079 coherent                       p_from_t

Reading the check output:

Part Meaning
First line The numbers are consistent or inconsistent with each other.
Level 0 to 3 How much could be checked: 0 nothing; 1 statistic, df and p against each other; 2 the statistic recomputed from the descriptives; 3 the whole sufficient set is reported.
verified An output (t, df) was recomputed from more basic numbers and matches.
coherent The number fits the others, but only as an input to a check, or through numbers derived from other numbers.
inconsistent The number is in a relation that fails under every variant, or in relations no single analysis choice satisfies together.
not checkable No relation of this test reaches the number.
unconfirmed The number’s relation could not be evaluated because another input is missing.
Missing numbers If a number was not reported but the others constrain it, its implied range is shown.

A set of numbers that cannot all be right is reported as inconsistent:

check_reported("paired", n = "20", t = "2.85", df = "19", p = ".050")
#> The analysis is inconsistent with the reported statistics.
#> Level 1: internal coherence only (statistic, df, p and CI are checked against each other, not against the descriptives).
#> Variants that fit: none
#> 
#>  quantity reported       status     checked_against
#>         n       20     coherent           df_from_n
#>         t     2.85 inconsistent            p_from_t
#>        df       19 inconsistent df_from_n; p_from_t
#>         p     .050 inconsistent            p_from_t
#> 
#> An inconsistency shows the numbers cannot all be correct as reported, not which one is wrong or why.
#> Also report m, sd and r (together, to level 3) to make this fully checkable.

The R squared family is checked too: a Pearson correlation reported as .40 for 32 cases, with an R squared of .30, cannot be right: R squared is the square of the correlation.

check_reported("pearson", n = "32", r = "0.40", r2 = "0.30")$consistent
#> [1] FALSE

“Inconsistent” means the numbers cannot all be correct as reported. It does not say which number is wrong, or why: a typo, a different test, a different rounding or a real mistake all look the same. check_reported() names the test first: "student", "welch", "one_sample", "paired", "pearson", "oneway", "factorial", "chisq", "gof", "mediation", "lm", "lm_simple" or "lm_moderation".

Documentation

The reference and these articles are on the package website.

  • Get started, or vignette("reprokit"): getting started, one worked example for authors and one for readers.
  • Concepts and terms, or vignette("concepts"): what the terms mean (sufficient set, APA set, coverage level, verdicts, rounding intervals, and so on).
  • Validation, or vignette("validation"): the evidence behind the claims, and the scripts that produce it.

What it covers

Version 0.1.0 covers, for share, check and appendix alike:

  • chi-squared tests of independence and goodness of fit;
  • one-sample, independent-samples (Student and Welch) and paired-samples t;
  • Pearson correlation;
  • one-way and factorial (two-factor) between-subjects ANOVA;
  • simple, multiple and moderation regression, and simple mediation.

Everything else gets a verdict only: a verdict and advice, but no stored statistics and no check (repeated-measures ANOVA, logistic and Poisson regression, SEM, rank tests and Spearman, standalone effect sizes, multilevel and mixed models, GEE).

coverage_table() lists, for each test, the numbers APA style reports, the sufficient set, what is missing from the APA set, what can be checked and what cannot (with the reason), and the choices you have to declare. The table below is generated from the handler registry when this README is built, so it is the reference, not a copy:

test verdict apa sufficient missing covered checkable not_checkable choices extras
Pearson correlation test apa_suffices n, M, SD per variable, r, df, p, CI n, r — — df, p, CI M, SD per variable (r does not depend on them) tails (two-sided, one-sided (less), one-sided (greater)); confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%) R², adjusted R²
Paired-samples t-test apa_plus_suffices n, M, SD per condition, t, df, p, d, CI n, M, SD per condition, r r (the SD of the differences depends on the correlation between conditions; per-condition M and SD do not determine it) — t, df, p, d, CI — tails (two-sided, one-sided (less), one-sided (greater)); confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%); effect-size convention (d_z (SD of the differences), d_rm (repeated measures), d_av (average SD), g_av (average SD, Hedges’ correction), eta squared, omega squared); direction of the difference: first minus second in Pair(first, second) eta2, R², omega2
Moderation apa_plus_suffices n, M, SD per variable, b, SE, t, p, CI, R², F, df1, df2, model p n, M, SD per variable, the correlations, the X·Z moments the correlations (coefficients depend on how the predictors overlap); the X·Z moments (cannot be derived from X and Z summaries) — b, SE, t, p, CI, R², F, df1, df2, model p — confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%); effect-size convention (R², adjusted R²); centering; coding standardized beta
Multiple regression apa_plus_suffices n, M, SD per variable, b, SE, t, p, CI, R², F, df1, df2, model p n, M, SD per variable, the correlations the correlations (coefficients depend on how the predictors overlap) — b, SE, t, p, CI, R², F, df1, df2, model p — confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%); effect-size convention (R², adjusted R²); factor coding standardized beta
Simple mediation apa_plus_suffices n, M, SD per variable, b, SE, t, p, CI, a·b and its CI n, M, SD and correlations of X, M, Y the correlations of X, M, Y — a, b, c, c′ (b, SE, t, p, CI each) the CI of a·b (inferred by bootstrap, which resamples cases; summaries cannot) confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%) R², F
Simple regression apa_suffices n, M, SD per variable, b, SE, t, p, CI, R², F, df1, df2, model p n, M, SD per variable, r — r (standardized β, sign(b)·√R², or t/√(t²+df)) b, SE, t, p, CI, R², F, df1, df2, model p — confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%); effect-size convention (R², adjusted R²) standardized beta
Chi-squared goodness of fit apa_plus_suffices the observed counts, chisq, df, p, N the observed counts, H0 proportions H0 proportions (the expected counts depend on them; not needed when they are equal) — chisq, df, p, N — effect-size convention (Cohen’s w) —
Chi-squared test of independence apa_suffices the contingency table, chisq, df, p, N, V the contingency table — — chisq, df, p, N, V — test (Pearson chi-squared, Yates’ continuity correction); effect-size convention (Cramér’s V) —
Factorial ANOVA, two factors (between-subjects) apa_suffices n, M, SD per condition, F, df1, df2, p, partial eta2 n, M, SD per condition — — F, df1, df2, p, partial eta2 — SS type for unbalanced designs (type III, type II, type I); effect-size convention (partial eta squared, partial omega squared) partial eta2, partial omega2
Independent-samples t-test (Student, Welch) apa_suffices n, M, SD per condition, t, df, p, d, CI n, M, SD per condition — — t, df, p, d, CI — tails (two-sided, one-sided (less), one-sided (greater)); confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%); test (Student’s t, Welch’s t); effect-size convention (Cohen’s d (pooled SD), Hedges’ g, Cohen’s d (root mean square of the SDs), Glass’s Δ (SD of the first group), Glass’s Δ (SD of the second group), eta squared, omega squared) eta2, R², omega2
One-sample t-test apa_suffices n, M, SD, t, df, p, d, CI n, M, SD — — t, df, p, d, CI — tails (two-sided, one-sided (less), one-sided (greater)); confidence level (90%, 95%, 99%); effect-size convention (Cohen’s d, Hedges’ g, eta squared, omega squared); test value mu (default 0) eta2, R², omega2
One-way ANOVA (between-subjects) apa_suffices n, M, SD per condition, F, df1, df2, p, eta2 n, M, SD per condition — — F, df1, df2, p, eta2 — effect-size convention (eta squared, omega squared); variance assumption: equal variances (classical F test, not Welch’s) R², omega2

A one-way ANOVA is checked with check_reported("oneway", ...) (note the lowercase f for the statistic): per-group n, mean and SD, plus F, both df, eta squared and p.

check_reported("oneway", n = c("10", "10", "10"), m = c("5.03", "4.66", "5.53"),
               sd = c("0.58", "0.79", "0.44"),
               f = "4.85", df1 = "2", df2 = "27", eta2 = "0.26", p = ".016")
#> The analysis is consistent with the reported statistics.
#> Level 3: the sufficient set is reported (the numbers contain everything needed to reproduce the analysis; that is not itself a check).
#> Effect-size conventions that fit: eta squared
#> 
#>  quantity         reported   status                             checked_against
#>         n       10, 10, 10 coherent df1_from_n; df2_from_n; f_from_descriptives
#>         m 5.03, 4.66, 5.53 coherent                         f_from_descriptives
#>        sd 0.58, 0.79, 0.44 coherent                         f_from_descriptives
#>         f             4.85 verified  f_from_descriptives; p_from_f; eta2_from_f
#>       df1                2 verified           df1_from_n; p_from_f; eta2_from_f
#>       df2               27 verified           df2_from_n; p_from_f; eta2_from_f
#>      eta2             0.26 coherent                                 eta2_from_f
#>         p             .016 coherent                                    p_from_f

A two-factor between-subjects ANOVA is checked with check_reported("factorial", ...), one effect at a time: pass the cell n, M and SD as a x b matrices (rows are the levels of A, columns the levels of B) and name the effect ("A", "B" or "AB"). In an unbalanced design the sums of squares type (III, II or I) is a choice the report must settle; the output lists the types that fit. Partial eta squared and partial omega squared are conventions.

cells <- matrix(rep("10", 4), 2)
check_reported("factorial", n = cells, m = matrix(c("4.10", "5.20", "4.80", "7.40"), 2),
               sd = matrix(rep("1.50", 4), 2), effect = "A",
               f = "15.21", df1 = "1", df2 = "36", p = "< .001", eta2 = ".30")
#> The analysis is consistent with the reported statistics.
#> Level 3: the sufficient set is reported (the numbers contain everything needed to reproduce the analysis; that is not itself a check).
#> Effect-size conventions that fit: partial eta squared
#> 
#>  quantity               reported   status
#>         n         10, 10, 10, 10 coherent
#>         m 4.10, 5.20, 4.80, 7.40 coherent
#>        sd 1.50, 1.50, 1.50, 1.50 coherent
#>         f                  15.21 verified
#>       df1                      1 coherent
#>       df2                     36 verified
#>         p                 < .001 verified
#>      eta2                    .30 coherent
#>                                            checked_against
#>       df2_from_n; f_from_descriptives; p_from_descriptives
#>                   f_from_descriptives; p_from_descriptives
#>                   f_from_descriptives; p_from_descriptives
#>  df1_from_dims; f_from_descriptives; p_from_f; eta2_from_f
#>                       df1_from_dims; p_from_f; eta2_from_f
#>                          df2_from_n; p_from_f; eta2_from_f
#>                              p_from_descriptives; p_from_f
#>                                                eta2_from_f
#> 
#> Note: Effect checked: A (the factor in the rows of the cell matrices).

A chi-squared test is checked with check_reported("chisq", ...) ("gof" for goodness of fit): pass the table as a matrix (a vector for goodness of fit) and the reported numbers. Yates’ correction is a variant, Cramer’s V a convention.

check_reported("chisq", n = matrix(c("30", "10", "20", "40"), 2), chisq = "15.04",
               df = "1", p = ".0001", v = ".41")
#> The analysis is consistent with the reported statistics.
#> Level 3: the sufficient set is reported (the numbers contain everything needed to reproduce the analysis; that is not itself a check).
#> Tests that fit: Yates' continuity correction
#> Effect-size conventions that fit: none
#> 
#>  quantity       reported   status                              checked_against
#>         n 30, 10, 20, 40 coherent chisq_from_table; p_from_table; v_from_table
#>     chisq          15.04 verified chisq_from_table; df_from_dims; p_from_chisq
#>        df              1 coherent                   df_from_dims; p_from_chisq
#>         p          .0001 verified                   p_from_table; p_from_chisq
#>         v            .41 verified                                 v_from_table

A regression is checked with check_reported("lm", ...), with one named value per term; use "lm_simple" or "lm_moderation" for those rows. Simple mediation is checked with check_reported("mediation", ...), which checks the paths a, b, c and c’ and the indirect effect against the product of the a and b rounding intervals. It says “not coherent” if they cannot co-occur (a bootstrap mean can differ a little); the indirect effect’s interval is not checkable.

check_reported("lm", b = c(wt = "-3.19", hp = "-0.04"), se = c(wt = "0.64", hp = "0.01"),
               t = c(wt = "-5.00", hp = "-3.67"), df2 = "29", k = 2)
#> The analysis is consistent with the reported statistics.
#> Level 1: internal coherence only (statistic, df, p and CI are checked against each other, not against the descriptives).
#> 
#>  quantity reported        status checked_against
#>      b:wt    -3.19      coherent  t_from_b_se:wt
#>      b:hp    -0.04      coherent  t_from_b_se:hp
#>     se:wt     0.64      coherent  t_from_b_se:wt
#>     se:hp     0.01      coherent  t_from_b_se:hp
#>      t:wt    -5.00      coherent  t_from_b_se:wt
#>      t:hp    -3.67      coherent  t_from_b_se:hp
#>       df2       29 not checkable               -
#> 
#> Derived from the reported numbers: n = 32 (from df2).
#> Also report m, sd and r_all (together, to level 3) to make this fully checkable.

Status and limits

reprokit is version 0.1.0, the first release, with lifecycle “experimental”: function names and output may still change. In this version:

  • It checks whether reported numbers agree with each other. It does not check whether the analysis was appropriate, whether the data are plausible, or which number is wrong.
  • It cannot replace the raw data. For analyses where summaries do not suffice, or that are outside the list above, sufficient_stats() says so (needs_raw_data) and lists the alternatives; appendix() refuses.
  • The disclosure check flags groups, cells, categories and factor levels with fewer than 5 cases (the default threshold). It lowers the risk of identifying a participant; it never removes it, and passing it is not a guarantee of anonymity.
  • The evidence for the claims is in inst/validation/; each script writes its result to inst/validation/results/, and vignette("validation") shows them.

Reporting bugs

Please open an issue at https://github.com/dm-k1/reprokit/issues. A minimal example with the reported numbers as strings helps most.

Prior art

reprokit builds on these rather than replacing them:

  • statcheck (Nuijten and Epskamp): recomputes p values from reported test statistics.
  • JATSdecoder get.stats() (Böschen): extracts statistical results from articles.
  • scrutiny (Jung): error detection for reported summary statistics, including GRIM.
  • rsprite2 (Wallrich): SPRITE, reconstructing possible samples from a mean and SD.
  • unsum and CLOSURE (Jung): the same reconstruction, by exhaustive search.
  • Nick Brown’s f_range(): the range of F values consistent with rounded means and SDs.
  • RIVETS (Brown and Heathers): a checklist for detecting problems in a study report.
  • synthpop (Nowok, Raab and Dibben): synthetic data.
  • faux (DeBruine): simulating data from a specified structure.
  • DataSHIELD: analysis without moving the data.
  • metacheck (DeBruine, Lakens and others): automated checks of reported results.
